traveler: Haydée Tamara Bunke Bíder (Tania la Guerrillera)
title: Once to Vado del Yeso: the Argentine Girl from the German Exile, and the Woman Who Went Under
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Buenos Aires, a daughter registered in Once
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the barrio of Once, at the corner of Corrientes and Pasteur, Erich Bunke and Nadia Bíder register a daughter on the nineteenth of November 1937 and name her Haydée Tamara. Both parents carry Communist Party cards. Both left Germany when staying became a way of dying. Their apartment fills with exiled militants and three languages cross one table. This is the Buenos Aires that Ernesto Guevara will leave on a motorcycle fifteen years from now, and the city Fidel Castro will address in 1959, four months after taking Havana. No plaque marks the corner. The child learns to read in German and in Spanish at once.
suggested_refs: The corner of Corrientes and Pasteur, barrio de Once, Buenos Aires
The family's later address at Sarmiento 2106

stops.name: Escuela Cangallo, the father at the front of the room
stops.date_confidence: approximate: the primary years run about 1944 to 1949, and no enrollment record was reached; the day and month are placeholders
stops.campa: At the school on the street then called Cangallo, now Teniente General Juan Domingo Perón 2169, Tamara Bunke does her primary schooling among the children of the immigrant left. Her father teaches in the same building. The household runs two curricula at once: Argentine civics by day, and at home the grammar and the songs of a country the family was driven out of and refuses to lose. Sources disagree already about where the Bunkes came from, one calling the mother a communist Jew from Russia, another calling her Polish. The girl answers to a name in two languages and hears both spoken about her.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Cangallo building at Juan Domingo Perón 2169, Balvanera, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Quilmes, the Club Vorwärts
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the club is attested through her father's board membership, the years of the family's attendance are not, and the club's historical address was not verified
stops.campa: South of the capital, in Quilmes, the German émigré sports and culture club Vorwärts gives the Bunkes a second house. Erich Bunke sits on its board. Gymnastics and choir practice double as the organizing of the anti-fascist German colony in Argentina, a colony that treats Buenos Aires as one address among several and expects to use the others again. Tamara grows up inside it, learning internationalism at the age other children learn table manners. Nothing in her later life reads as a conversion.
suggested_refs: The Club Vorwärts of the German anti-fascist emigration, Quilmes, Buenos Aires province

stops.name: Escuela Normal N.9, the last Argentine classroom
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the school is named by Spanish Wikipedia, its building and the years of attendance are not attested and the coordinate is a general Buenos Aires pin
stops.campa: She goes on to the Escuela Normal N.9, into the normalista tradition that made generations of Argentine teachers. Classmates remember a serious girl, disciplined, already carrying her parents' politics as her own. Here the record forks and cannot be closed: the Spanish account has her joining an Argentine communist youth federation in 1951, while the English account has her joining the Free German Youth in Germany the same year, two years before she can possibly have been there. Within two years the family will leave Argentina. This classroom closes behind her for good.
suggested_refs: Escuela Normal N.9, Buenos Aires, building unverified

stops.name: Stalinstadt, arrival in the first socialist city
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by English and German Wikipedia; EcuRed gives 1951 instead, and no source gives a month or a day
stops.campa: The family leaves Argentina for the German Democratic Republic and settles in Stalinstadt, the republic's first planned socialist city, raised around a new steelworks on the Oder within sight of the Polish border. Erich Bunke teaches there. Tamara is fourteen and arrives speaking German with an accent, an outsider among children who have never left the country. She joins the Free German Youth. The town will later shed Stalin and become Eisenhüttenstadt, but nothing later undoes the first Central European winter after a childhood in Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: Stalinstadt, now Eisenhüttenstadt, and the Eisenhüttenkombinat Ost

stops.name: Eisenhüttenstadt, the letters to the other country
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated only to 1956 by the source that quotes it, and the day and month are unknown; she takes her Abitur the same year
stops.campa: She takes her Abitur in 1956 and, at eighteen, is admitted to the Socialist Unity Party, the one point on which the German, Spanish, and Cuban accounts of her life agree without argument. She is also writing to Argentina. The letters that survive in quotation are not homesick; they are administrative and impatient, asking after party work and youth work in a country she still calls hers, and setting a date for going back. The date will pass. She keeps five languages in working order and does not yet know what any of them are for.
stops.quote: ¿Podéis escribirme sobre el trabajo del Partido y en especial de la juventud allá en la Argentina?
stops.quote_source: Letter of Tamara Bunke, 1956, to an unnamed friend, quoted in Lois Pérez Leira, 'Tamara Bunke Bíder: Tania la Guerrillera', Diario 16, 2 September 2017, via Spanish Wikipedia
suggested_refs: The 1956 and 1957 letters quoted by Lois Pérez Leira, originals not located

stops.name: East Berlin, Humboldt University and file 430/60
stops.date_confidence: the matriculation year is attested by German Wikipedia; the month is unknown, and English and Spanish Wikipedia give the faculty differently as philosophy and as letters
stops.campa: At Humboldt University on Unter den Linden she enrolls in the Romance languages institute and interprets for Latin American delegations passing through the capital. She shoots competitively and collects medals for it. By 1960 the foreign intelligence arm of the Ministry for State Security has opened a file on her under the category of prospective agent, number 430/60. Her professors are producing a philologist. Something on the other side of the city is producing an asset. Nobody tells her which of the two careers has already been chosen.
suggested_refs: Stasi Perspektivagentin file 430/60, cited by German Wikipedia, archival reference not reached

stops.name: Vienna, the VII World Festival of Youth and Students
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by Spanish Wikipedia, which gives no month for her travel; the day and month are placeholders
stops.campa: She travels to Vienna with an Argentine delegation for the VII World Festival of Youth and Students, the bloc's recurring parade of young communists, folk dancers, and delegations from the decolonizing world. It is her first working immersion in the choreography of official friendship: flags, translation booths, banquets held for the sake of the photographs. Cuba is there in the crowds, not two years past the fall of Batista and not yet certain what it is. Eighteen months from now a Cuban trade delegation in Leipzig will need an interpreter.
suggested_refs: The VII World Festival of Youth and Students, Vienna, 1959

stops.name: Leipzig, the interpreter meets the trade delegation
stops.date_confidence: Spanish Wikipedia narrows the meeting to December 1960; English Wikipedia gives only the year, and no source gives a day
stops.campa: In Leipzig she is assigned as interpreter to a visiting Cuban delegation and meets Ernesto Guevara, minister of a government two years old, touring the socialist bloc for trade and machinery. The rapport is immediate and rests on nothing more mysterious than a shared language and a shared analysis. She also interprets for the ballerina Alicia Alonso, who invites her to Havana. She decides that winter not to go back to Argentina. A handshake at a trade fair in an East German industrial town starts the line that ends on a Bolivian riverbank.
suggested_refs: The Leipzig trade fair and the Cuban delegation of 1960

stops.name: Prague, the waypoint
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia attests a 1961 transit through Prague on the route to Havana; the month and day are unknown
stops.campa: She passes through Prague on the corridor that bloc travelers use to reach Cuba before direct flights are common. The stop is administrative: visas, connections, a night in a city that keeps records of everyone. She will come back to this same place three years from now under another name and for another purpose, and Guevara himself will spend a hidden winter outside it in 1966, disguised and studying the maps of Bolivia. Prague enters her file twice, once as a waiting room and once as a school, and she does not choose either visit.
suggested_refs: The Prague transit corridor of socialist-bloc travel to Havana, 1961

stops.name: Havana, arrival in an armed city
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twelfth of May 1961 she lands in Havana on the ballet's invitation, three weeks after the invaders at the Bay of Pigs were beaten in seventy-two hours. The city is triumphant and armed at the same time. She takes Cuban citizenship, works across the young state's institutions, and describes the period afterwards in the flat vocabulary of a militant rather than of a convert. Havana will hold her for three years. What it wants from her in the end is not her German, not her Spanish, and not her party card, but her face, which no Bolivian has seen.
stops.quote: became directly involved in revolutionary activities
stops.quote_source: Tamara Bunke, Autobiographical Note (published 2005), p. 152, quoted in English Wikipedia; a second quoted fragment, grassroots organizations, follows in the same sentence
suggested_refs: Tamara Bunke's Autobiographical Note, published 2005, not fetched

stops.name: University of Havana, journalism at night
stops.date_confidence: the enrollment falls somewhere in the Havana years 1961 to 1963; no source gives a start date, and the day and month are placeholders
stops.campa: She enrolls to study journalism at the University of Havana, in classrooms a revolution two years old is still rearranging. She works for the state by day and studies at night, a pattern colleagues later describe as her ordinary speed rather than an exertion. Her Spanish is a Buenos Aires childhood, her German is a Stalinstadt adolescence, and her Russian is good enough to be useful; the foreign delegations moving through the city need all three. The credential she is earning is real. It is also the last public document she will hold under her own name.
suggested_refs: The University of Havana campus, Vedado

stops.name: Havana, the Ministry, ICAP, and the Federation
stops.date_confidence: the posts run across 1961 to 1963; the October 1962 date marks the missile crisis in Fidel Castro's Havana, not a dated event in her own file
stops.campa: Across the Ministry of Education, the Cuban Institute of Friendship with Peoples, and the Federation of Cuban Women she builds the paper trail of an ordinary revolutionary functionary: reports, translations, the logistics of visiting delegations. It is also an apprenticeship. ICAP handles the traffic of foreign sympathizers and cadres through the island, which trains her to hold a room of strangers who do not know one another's business, and to remember every face in it. In October 1962 the city she works in spends thirteen days expecting to be destroyed.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Cubano de Amistad con los Pueblos (ICAP), Havana

stops.name: Havana, the training begins
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia dates the start of the DGI training to May 1963; the day is unknown and the safe house is not named in any reachable source
stops.campa: From May 1963 she trains with the Dirección General de Inteligencia in Havana under the officer Ulises Estrada, with whom she also begins a relationship. The curriculum is clandestine communication, surveillance detection, and the construction of a legend solid enough to hold for years under a foreign government's eyes. The house where this happens is not named in any source that can be read. By early 1964 she has been selected for a mission whose target she has not been told, in a country where no guerrilla has yet fired a shot.
suggested_refs: Ulises Estrada, Tania: Undercover with Che Guevara in Bolivia, not fetched

stops.name: Cienfuegos, the war name
stops.date_confidence: EcuRed dates the completion of the first training phase to 20 February 1964 and the transfer to Cienfuegos after it; accounts that put Cienfuegos in 1963 invert that order
stops.campa: The first phase closes on the twentieth of February 1964 and she is transferred to Cienfuegos for the physical and paramilitary half of the preparation. In the bay that once held a Spanish colonial arsenal she takes the name she will die under: Tania, for Zoya Kosmodemyanskaya, the eighteen-year-old Soviet partisan the Germans hanged in Petrishchevo in 1941 and who gave a false name to her interrogators. Haydée Tamara Bunke Bíder is filed away in a drawer in Havana. Cienfuegos raises no monument to a woman who was never officially there.
suggested_refs: The Cienfuegos training installations, unlocated in open sources

stops.name: Havana, departure under another name
stops.date_confidence: attested by EcuRed
stops.campa: On the ninth of April 1964 she leaves Havana on a passport that does not carry her name, bound for Europe by a route designed to be boring. She will not see the island again. The method requires her to spend months laundering an identity through customs halls and hotel registers until the paper trail behind Laura Gutiérrez Bauer is longer and duller than the truth. Everyone she has worked with in three years of Cuban life is told nothing. The last person to see Tamara Bunke leave is a passport officer who reads a different name and waves her through.
suggested_refs: EcuRed's day-exact chronology of the clandestine years, resting on Cuban intelligence memoirs

stops.name: Prague, the second visit
stops.date_confidence: German Wikipedia gives spring 1964 for the Czechoslovak training; the month here is placed after the 9 April departure from Havana and is not itself attested
stops.campa: She returns to Prague, this time for instruction by the Czechoslovak State Security service, a routine loan of expertise between Warsaw Pact services and their Cuban partners. What she was taught in those weeks is not recorded anywhere that can be read; the fact and the season are all that survive. Three years earlier she crossed this city carrying her own passport and her own history. She leaves it now carrying neither, moving west toward the capitalist bloc with each layer of the cover thickened by another set of stamps.
suggested_refs: Czechoslovak StB assistance to Cuban intelligence operations, course records not reached

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the cover completed
stops.date_confidence: attested by EcuRed; the claim is frequently miscited to Spanish Wikipedia, in whose text Frankfurt does not appear
stops.campa: On the fifth of August 1964 she arrives in Frankfurt am Main on a passport reading Haydée Bider González, and in West Germany completes the last change: from that document into Laura Gutiérrez Bauer, Argentine, ethnologist, unmarried, of independent means and academic curiosity. The country of her parents' exile serves as the final airlock. A German woman raised in Argentina now enters the world as an Argentine woman with a German surname, which is close enough to true to survive questioning and false enough to be worth killing her for.
suggested_refs: The passport identity Haydée Bider González, per EcuRed

stops.name: La Paz, the ethnologist takes a room
stops.date_confidence: October 1964 per English and German Wikipedia; EcuRed instead dates 5 November 1964 to her arrival in Peru before the border crossing, and no source gives a day for La Paz
stops.campa: She comes into Bolivia and builds Laura Gutiérrez Bauer into a working life at three thousand six hundred metres: German tutor, folklore researcher, freelance journalist, a foreign woman who is interested in everything and threatening to nobody. La Paz accepts her. Within months she moves among ministry officials, army officers, diplomats, painters, and the daughters of good families, and reports what she learns to handlers she meets by arrangement. The war she is preparing the ground for has not been decided on yet in Havana, and she is already two years ahead of it.
suggested_refs: The identity papers of Laura Gutiérrez Bauer, Argentine ethnologist

stops.name: La Paz, residency, passport, and a husband
stops.date_confidence: 20 January 1965 is EcuRed's date for the permanent residency and the Bolivian passport; Spanish Wikipedia names the marriage to Mario Martínez but gives it neither a date nor a city, and the two facts are often wrongly welded together
stops.campa: On the twentieth of January 1965 she holds permanent residency and a Bolivian passport. She has also married Mario Martínez, a student of electrical engineering, which is the ordinary way a foreign woman becomes a citizen and the reason the marriage is recorded at all. Whether anything besides paperwork passed between them is disputed by her biographers and settled by none of them. She is now a Bolivian in law, and a Bolivian passport is the one document that lets her cross her own borders without a story.
suggested_refs: The Bolivian residency and passport of Laura Gutiérrez Bauer, January 1965

stops.name: La Paz, a desk inside the palace
stops.date_confidence: the post spans 1965 and 1966; 1 January 1966 is the attested date of her meeting with the contact called Mercy, and the start of the palace employment is not dated
stops.campa: She takes work as secretary to the press spokesman in the Bolivian presidential palace, which puts her every working day inside the information apparatus of the government her service intends to bring down. She wins the trust of General Alfredo Ovando and of President René Barrientos himself. On the first of January 1966 she meets a contact recorded only as Mercy. The network she is assembling now has two ends: at one, the men who sign the army's orders, and at the other, a war being planned in Havana that has no soldiers and no ground yet.
suggested_refs: The Palacio Quemado press office, La Paz

stops.name: Mexico City, the clandestine interviews
stops.date_confidence: April 1966 per EcuRed, which gives no day; the trip is frequently miscited to Spanish Wikipedia, in whose text it does not appear
stops.campa: In April 1966 she travels to Mexico City for clandestine meetings on the preparation of the guerrilla mission. Mexico has held this office before: a decade earlier, in a house in this city, eighty-two men trained under a Spanish Civil War veteran and sailed for Cuba on the Granma. She is now part of the same apparatus running the same play on new ground. She receives what she is given, says nothing to anyone in La Paz, and is back in Bolivia the following month with her ethnological research apparently uninterrupted.
suggested_refs: The Cuban clandestine apparatus in Mexico City, 1966

stops.name: La Paz, the urban network
stops.date_confidence: May 1966 per EcuRed for the liaison contact and the return from Mexico; the day is unknown
stops.campa: Back in the capital by May 1966 she intensifies the work: safe houses, couriers, people who can move money and medicine without being noticed doing it. The double life holds. She is still the researcher with an interest in folklore, invited to the right dinners, while the machinery underneath her turns military. What the network lacks is drivers. Within a year she will make the runs south herself, in her own vehicle, which is the one task her cover was never built to survive.
suggested_refs: The urban support network of the Bolivian ELN, La Paz, 1966

stops.name: Camiri, the houses near the oil town
stops.date_confidence: attested by EcuRed; the claim is often miscited to Spanish Wikipedia, in which Camiri does not appear
stops.campa: On the tenth of July 1966 she secures safe houses in and around Camiri, the oil town of Santa Cruz department nearest the broken country where the camp will be. The houses are the hinge between the capital and the future front: a relay for people, weapons, and supplies moving south under the cover of ordinary oil traffic. Camiri is a good choice because nothing happens there worth reporting. Within a year the same town will hold the interrogation cells, and the vehicle that ends her cover will be found near one of these addresses.
suggested_refs: Camiri, Santa Cruz department, headquarters of the Bolivian 4th Division

stops.name: La Paz, Hotel Copacabana, the bald economist checks in
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date is inherited from the atlas record of Che Guevara's journey, in which this stop and its coordinate already stand
stops.campa: A balding, bespectacled economist of the Organization of American States, travelling as Adolfo Mena González, checks into room 504 of the Hotel Copacabana on the Prado. He photographs himself in the wardrobe mirror with a pipe in his hand. Nobody looks twice, and nobody looks twice because two years of a woman's patient work have made this city safe for him to walk into. Ernesto Guevara enters Bolivia through a door Tania built and does not have to knock. Four days from now, in a canyon four hundred kilometres away, he will name her in the first line of the last diary.
suggested_refs: The self-portrait of Che disguised as Adolfo Mena González, Hotel Copacabana, November 1966
sources: che_guevara.journey.json, stop 'La Paz, Hotel Copacabana, the bald economist' (1966-11-03)

stops.name: Ñancahuazú, the Casa de Calamina, the woman come down from La Paz
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date and the coordinate are inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json, which names Tania at this stop
stops.campa: On the seventh of November 1966 the tin-roofed farmhouse on the Ñancahuazú river receives the men who will call themselves the Ejército de Liberación Nacional, the name Camilo Torres Restrepo's Colombian guerrilla took twenty months earlier from the same grandfather in Havana. Guevara rules a fresh notebook and writes that a new stage begins. Around him are Cuban comandantes of the Sierra, Bolivian miners, Régis Debray, Ciro Bustos, and the woman Tania come down from her deep cover in La Paz society. She is the only German in the canyon and nobody there knows it.
suggested_refs: The Casa de Calamina at Ñancahuazú
El Diario del Che en Bolivia, opening entry, 7 November 1966
sources: che_guevara.journey.json, stop 'Ñancahuazú, the Casa de Calamina' (1966-11-07)
camilo_torres_restrepo.journey.json, stop on the ELN naming

stops.name: Ñancahuazú, delivering the general secretary
stops.date_confidence: December 1966 per EcuRed, which gives no day; the participant accounts behind the escort role were not fetched
stops.campa: In December she drives Mario Monje, general secretary of the Bolivian Communist Party, from La Paz to the camp. Monje asks for political and military command of a war on his own country's soil; Guevara refuses to give up either. The two men part having agreed on nothing, and Bolivian communist support fractures before a shot is fired. Tania has delivered the meeting that costs the campaign its only national organization. She drives back to the capital, resumes the ethnologist, and files her report on a conversation that has already decided how this ends.
suggested_refs: The Monje meeting at Ñancahuazú, December 1966

stops.name: Ñancahuazú, the last delivery
stops.date_confidence: March 1967 per EcuRed for the trip carrying Debray and Bustos; the day is not given
stops.campa: In March 1967 she makes her last run for the urban network, carrying the French philosopher Régis Debray and the Argentine painter Ciro Bustos toward the camp. It is not a courier's job and she is not a courier; she is the most valuable embedded asset the operation has, spending herself on transport because there is nobody else left to do it. She reaches the guerrilla zone. Behind her, on a road she has driven a dozen times without incident, the two and a half years of Laura Gutiérrez Bauer are about to end in a parked vehicle.
suggested_refs: The March 1967 transport of Debray and Bustos to the guerrilla zone

stops.name: Camiri, the jeep and the address book
stops.date_confidence: March 1967 per German Wikipedia, which records the vehicle's discovery and the blown cover; the day is unknown, and English Wikipedia does not name Camiri as the safe house where the jeep stood
stops.campa: A captured Bolivian communist gives up a safe house. In its yard stands her jeep, and in the jeep is her address book with the names and the papers that identify Laura Gutiérrez Bauer. Everything falls at once: the researcher, the tutor, the secretary in the palace press office, the guest at the general's table. The army now has a photograph and a list. The urban network she spent two and a half years assembling is rolled up behind her, and there is no road left in Bolivia that she can drive under her own registration.
suggested_refs: The captured address book of Laura Gutiérrez Bauer, March 1967

stops.name: Ñancahuazú, the diary counts the loss
stops.date_confidence: attested by the diary entry of 27 March 1967, seen only in German rendering
stops.campa: Guevara writes the loss into the diary on the twenty-seventh of March as a quartermaster writes off stores: two years of good and patient work, gone. He is not blaming her. He is recording what the column has just spent, and it has spent the one thing that made the campaign survivable, which was a woman in La Paz whom nobody suspected. Tania stays in the canyon because there is nowhere else. From this entry forward the guerrilla has no city, no intelligence, and no way back into the country it means to liberate.
stops.quote: zwei Jahre guter und geduldiger Arbeit verloren
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, diary entry of 27 March 1967, El Diario del Che en Bolivia, p. 341, in the German rendering carried by German Wikipedia; the Spanish original was not fetched
suggested_refs: El Diario del Che en Bolivia, entry of 27 March 1967, p. 341

stops.name: Muyupampa, the column splits
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date and the coordinate are inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json, which names Tania among the rearguard at this stop
stops.campa: To get its civilians out, the column maneuvers to Muyupampa so that Debray and Bustos can walk out as journalists. They are taken within hours and paraded, and the world learns that Guevara is alive and commanding in Bolivia. Green Berets arrive to raise a Ranger battalion and the CIA seconds its Cuban exile interrogators. In the same maneuvering the guerrilla splits: seventeen with Joaquín as rearguard, Tania among them, and the two halves will hunt for each other through the canyons for four months and never meet again.
suggested_refs: The capture of Debray and Bustos at Muyupampa, April 1967
sources: che_guevara.journey.json, stop 'Muyupampa, Debray and Bustos walk out' (1967-04-20)

stops.name: Masicuri, the rearguard in the broken country
stops.date_confidence: the leg injury, the fever, and the chigoe infestation are dated April 1967 and the Bella Vista duties June 1967 by the English chronology; the coordinate approximates a retreat corridor, since no campsite of these months is attested
stops.campa: She marches with Joaquín's rearguard through the hill and river country between Santa Cruz and Vallegrande, hunted by units closing from several directions, out of contact with Guevara for weeks at a time. She takes a leg injury, runs fevers, and is infested with chigoe fleas that have to be cut out of the feet. In the Bella Vista sector she works the radio, encrypts the messages nobody answers, and distributes the food there is not enough of. The intelligence officer is gone. What is left in the column is a soldier with a bad leg.
suggested_refs: The Río Grande and Masicuri retreat corridor of Joaquín's rearguard, 1967

stops.name: Vado del Yeso, the ford on the Río Grande
stops.date_confidence: attested; the ford itself has never been surveyed in the reachable literature and the coordinate is inherited from the atlas record of Che Guevara's journey rather than newly guessed
stops.campa: On the thirty-first of August the peasant Honorato Rojas, bought by the army, leads Joaquín's nine into the river at Vado del Yeso, near Puerto Mauricio, and steps aside. The soldiers are waiting on the bank. Tania is in the water when she is hit in the arm and the lung. The current takes her body and carries it downstream for days. She is twenty-nine. In her rucksack, when it is recovered, is an unfinished letter in German that no one in the Bolivian army can read, written by a woman who had run out of names for herself.
stops.quote: Ich weiß nicht, was aus mir werden soll. Wahrscheinlich nichts. Ich versuche mich daran zu erinnern, wie es ist, wenn man Courage hat. Ich bin ein Nichts. Ich bin nicht einmal mehr eine Frau, kein Mädchen, nur noch ein Kind.
stops.quote_source: Unfinished letter found in Tamara Bunke's rucksack after her death, quoted in Cordt Schnibben, 'Revolutionäre: Drei Leben in einer Haut', Der Spiegel, 23 September 1996, via German Wikipedia; the article itself was not fetched
suggested_refs: The ford at Vado del Yeso and Puerto Mauricio on the Río Grande
The rucksack letter, original not located

stops.name: Río Grande, the body recovered
stops.date_confidence: attested for the recovery date; the place on the river where the body came ashore is not fixed by any source and the ford's coordinate is reused
stops.campa: Six days after the ambush the army finds her in the river. Guevara, marching to a rendezvous that will never happen, hears of the annihilation of his rearguard on enemy radio and refuses it as psychological warfare, then hears the details again until they harden into fact. The last six weeks of his campaign are fought by a man who knows he is alone in the country. The soldiers who pull her out of the Río Grande have the highest-value corpse of the war and a name, Laura Gutiérrez Bauer, that stopped meaning anything in March.
suggested_refs: Bolivian army recovery reports on the Río Grande, September 1967

stops.name: Vallegrande, the unmarked grave
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the sources give only September 1967 and place the burial after the 6 September recovery; no source dates the burial itself
stops.campa: The body is brought to Vallegrande, shown to President René Barrientos with the other guerrilla dead, and put into unmarked ground at the edge of the town. Tradition in Vallegrande holds that local women intervened to see that she was buried as a Christian rather than dropped anonymously. Thirty-one years will pass before anyone digs her up and puts a name on her. Five weeks from now the same town will receive another body by helicopter and lay it out in a laundry room for the photographers, and the world will look at that one.
suggested_refs: The unmarked guerrilla graves at the periphery of Vallegrande

stops.name: La Higuera, the schoolhouse
stops.date_confidence: attested; the date and the coordinate are inherited byte-identical from che_guevara.journey.json
stops.campa: Thirty-nine days after Vado del Yeso, Ernesto Guevara is taken alive at the Quebrada del Yuro and shot the next morning in the schoolhouse at La Higuera by a sergeant who has to be given rum first. The counter-insurgency that closed the ford in August closes on him in October. The Bolivian campaign is over in eleven months, having liberated nothing. Both are put into unmarked ground in the same province, one of them famous and one of them not, and both stay there for thirty years.
suggested_refs: The schoolhouse at La Higuera, now a memorial
sources: che_guevara.journey.json, stops 'Quebrada del Yuro' and 'La Higuera, the schoolhouse, 9 October 1967'

stops.name: Río Grande, flowers on the thirty-first of August
stops.date_confidence: tradition, undated and recurring; EcuRed names no first year and 1968 stands here for the first anniversary
stops.campa: Every thirty-first of August, EcuRed says, unknown hands fill the place where her body was found with flowers. Nobody has ever recorded who they belong to, which is the point of the story and the reason it cannot be checked. Bolivia keeps her in the way it can. In 1999 a diving beetle collected in this country is described and given the name Desmopachria taniae, so that the alias she took in Cienfuegos for a hanged Russian girl of eighteen now belongs, in the literature, to an insect that lives in the water she died in.
stops.quote: Desde entonces, cada 31 de agosto, manos disconocidas llenan de flores aquel lugar donde se encontró su cuerpo.
stops.quote_source: EcuRed, 'Tamara Bunke Bíder'; the tradition is undated and unverifiable
suggested_refs: Desmopachria taniae, described from Bolivian material, 1999

stops.name: Dabel, the memorial stone in Mecklenburg
stops.date_confidence: the stone is dated 1984 by German Wikipedia, which gives no month or day
stops.campa: In the village of Dabel in Mecklenburg a stone is raised to her in 1984, seven years after the local group of the Democratic Women's League took her name. The German Democratic Republic that sent no one to Bolivia claims her thoroughly at home: more than two hundred schools, Free German Youth brigades, kindergartens, and a Berlin youth club carry the name of Tamara Bunke, who left the country in 1961 and never came back. The stone stands in a village of a few hundred people, in flat country, ten thousand kilometres from the river she died in.
suggested_refs: The 1984 Tamara Bunke memorial stone at Dabel, Landkreis Ludwigslust-Parchim

stops.name: Berlin, the names taken down
stops.date_confidence: the renamings follow the reunification of 1989 and 1990; the date given here stands for a process, not for a single decision
stops.campa: With the republic gone, nearly every institution that carried her name is renamed. The schools become other schools; the brigades cease to exist along with the organization that formed them. What survives the deletion is what nobody in Germany controls: minor planet 2283 Bunke, discovered in 1974, keeps its name in the sky, and in 1991 the Swiss director Heidi Specogna releases a documentary called Tania la Guerrillera. The GDR's daughter is struck off two hundred buildings in a single administrative season and stays on the ephemeris.
suggested_refs: Minor planet 2283 Bunke, discovered 26 September 1974
Heidi Specogna, Tania la Guerrillera, 1991

stops.name: Vallegrande, the general tells the truth
stops.date_confidence: November 1995 per English Wikipedia, which gives no day
stops.campa: In November 1995 the retired Bolivian general Mario Vargas Salinas states that Guevara's body was never cremated as the army said in 1967, and that it lies in the ground near the Vallegrande airstrip. He is the officer whose men mounted the ambush at Vado del Yeso. The confession opens a search that is looking for one famous man and finds, in the process, the ground where the others were put. Twenty-eight years after she was dropped into an unmarked pit, the state that killed her produces the witness who can say approximately where.
suggested_refs: The 1995 statement of Gen. Mario Vargas Salinas on the Vallegrande burials

stops.name: Vallegrande army base, the small pit
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia gives 13 October 1998; German Wikipedia dates the identification to September 1998 and Spanish Wikipedia gives only the year, and the month is contested
stops.campa: Her skeleton is found in a small pit at the edge of the Vallegrande army base and identified. Guevara's remains had been located the year before and were already in Cuba. The forensic work returns to a woman whose last three documents were all forgeries the name she was born with: Haydée Tamara Bunke Bíder, born in Buenos Aires in 1937. The base that buried her without a marker in 1967 is the address where the search finds her, which means the army always knew, and for thirty-one years nobody asked the army.
suggested_refs: The 1997-1998 Cuban and Bolivian forensic exhumations at Vallegrande

stops.name: Santa Clara, the mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: attested by the record of the Che Guevara Mausoleum, which dates this interment of ten guerrillas to 29 December 1998
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of December 1998 she is interred with nine other fighters of the Bolivian campaign in the mausoleum at Santa Clara, the city where Guevara's armored train action broke Batista's last line in 1958. The vault holds thirty in all, brought home in four groups between 1997 and 2000. Cuba gives a state funeral to a woman it sent out under another name to a country that was not hers, on the orders of a revolution that was not hers by birth either. The flame lit for the comandante burns over her as well.
suggested_refs: The Mausoleo del Che, Santa Clara, and its four groups of interments, 1997 to 2000

stops.name: Santiago de Cuba, the maternity hospital
stops.date_confidence: undated in the sources; the stop is placed after the 1998 repatriation as an editorial convenience and the naming may be much older
stops.campa: The Hospital Materno Norte in Santiago de Cuba carries her name, one of a set of Cuban institutions that do. The Venezuelan singer Alí Primera and the Chilean composer Patricio Manns each wrote a song for her, both of them addressed to Tania and not to Tamara Bunke. Cuba commemorates the alias, which is the part of her it made. Germany commemorated the name on the birth certificate. Argentina, where she was born and which she left at fourteen intending to return, has raised nothing at the corner of Corrientes and Pasteur.
suggested_refs: Hospital Materno Norte Tamara Bunke, Santiago de Cuba, dating unverified

stops.name: Berlin and Havana, the papers divided
stops.date_confidence: 2014 per German Wikipedia for the ICAP transfer; the month and day are unknown and the cataloguing at HTW Berlin is undated
stops.campa: Her estate is catalogued at the Berlin University of Applied Sciences under the researcher Oliver Rump, and in 2014 the association Cuba Sí hands part of her papers to the Cuban Institute of Friendship with Peoples in Havana, the same institution she once worked for as an ordinary translator of delegations. The archive ends up split between the two countries that claim her, in the two languages she was raised in at one table in Once. There are lines attributed to her that ask whether her name will be forgotten and answer, at least flowers and song. Whether she wrote them is not established.
stops.quote: So I must leave, like flowers that wilt? / Will my name one day be forgotten / And nothing of me remain on the earth? / At least, flowers and song.
stops.quote_source: Lines titled 'Leave a Memory', attributed to Tamara Bunke in Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life (1997), p. 689, via English Wikipedia; Anderson was not fetched, no date or place of composition is attested, and the lines closely echo the Nahuatl poem of the Cantares Mexicanos attributed to Nezahualcóyotl
suggested_refs: The Tamara Bunke papers at HTW Berlin and at ICAP, Havana
Jon Lee Anderson, Che Guevara: A Revolutionary Life (1997), p. 689
